entries.1e0a84fa97d9f60164fafa964cdd6a8d0e52514a: <div sID="gen22484" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Matt.15" sID="Matt.15"/> <div eID="gen22484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22486" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, we have our Lord Jesus, as the great Prophet teaching, as the great Physician healing, and as the great Shepherd of the sheep feeding; as the Father of spirits instructing them; as the Conqueror of Satan dispossessing him; and as concerned for the bodies of his people, providing for them. Here is, I. Christ's discourse with the scribes and Pharisees about human traditions and injunctions, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.1-Matt.15.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. His discourse with the multitude, and with his disciples, concerning the things that defile a man, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.10-Matt.15.20">ver. 10-20</reference>. III. His casting of the devil out of the woman of Canaan's daughter, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28">ver. 21-28</reference>. IV. His healing of all that were brought to him, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.29-Matt.15.31">ver. 29-31</reference>. V. His feeding of four thousand men, with seven loaves and a few little fishes, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.32-Matt.15.39">ver. 32-39</reference>.
entries.1b4a47a337d7e490c5fb341aa6700589290e6d8a: <div eID="gen22486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22485" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jesus Reproves the Scribes and Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen22487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then came to Jesus scribes and Pharisees, which were of Jerusalem, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Why do thy disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? for they wash not their hands when they eat bread. <hi type="super">3</hi> But he answered and said unto them, Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition? <hi type="super">4</hi> For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death. <hi type="super">5</hi> But ye say, Whosoever shall say to <hi type="italic">his</hi> father or <hi type="italic">his</hi> mother, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; <hi type="super">6</hi> And honour not his father or his mother, <hi type="italic">he shall be free.</hi> Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition. 7 <hi type="italic">Ye</hi> hypocrites, well did Esaias prophesy of you, saying, 8 This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with <hi type="italic">their</hi> lips; but their heart is far from me. <hi type="super">9</hi> But in vain they do worship me, teaching <hi type="italic">for</hi> doctrines the commandments of men. <div eID="gen22487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22488" type="x-p"/> Evil manners, we say, beget good laws. The intemperate heat of the Jewish teachers for the support of their hierarchy, occasioned many excellent discourses of our Saviour's for the settling of the truth, as here. <div eID="gen22488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22489" type="x-p"/> I. Here, is the cavil of the scribes and Pharisees at Christ's disciples, for <hi type="italic">eating with unwashen hands.</hi> The scribes and Pharisees were the great men of the Jewish church, men whose gain was godliness, great enemies to the gospel of Christ, but colouring their opposition with a pretence of zeal for the law of Moses, when really nothing was intended but the support of their own tyranny over the consciences of men. They were men of learning and men of business. These scribes and Pharisees here introduced were of Jerusalem, the holy city, the head city, whither <hi type="italic">the tribes went up,</hi> and where <hi type="italic">were set the thrones of judgment;</hi> they should therefore have been better than others, but they were worse. Note, External privileges, if they be not duly improved, commonly swell men up the more with pride and malignity. Jerusalem, which should have been a pure spring, was now become a poisoned sink. <hi type="italic">How is the faithful city become a harlot!</hi> <div eID="gen22489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22490" type="x-p"/> Now if these great men be the accusers, pray what is the accusation? What articles do they exhibit against the disciples of Christ? Why, truly, the thing laid to their charge, is, nonconformity to the canons of their church (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.2">v. 2</reference>); <hi type="italic">Why do thy disciples transgress the tradition of the elders?</hi> This charge they make good in a particular instance; <hi type="italic">They wash not their hands when they eat bread.</hi> A very high misdemeanor! It was a sign that Christ's disciples conducted themselves inoffensively, when this was the worst thing they could charge them with. <div eID="gen22490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22491" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. What was the <hi type="italic">tradition of the elders</hi>—That people should often wash their hands, and always at meat. This they placed a great deal of religion in, supposing that the meat they touched with unwashen hands would be defiling to them. The Pharisees practiced this themselves, and with a great deal of strictness imposed it upon others, not under civil penalties, but as matter of conscience, and making it a sin against God if they did not do it. Rabbi Joses determined, "that to eat with unwashen hands is as great a sin as adultery." And Rabbi Akiba being kept a close prisoner, having water sent him both to wash his hands with, and to drink with his meat, the greatest part being accidentally shed, he washed his hands with the remainder, though he left himself none to drink, saying he would rather die than transgress the tradition of the elders. Nay, they would not eat meat with one that did not wash before meat. This mighty zeal in so small a matter would appear very strange, if we did not still see it incident to church-oppressors, not only to be fond of practising their own inventions, but to be furious in pressing their own impositions. <div eID="gen22491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22492" type="x-p"/> 2. What was the transgression of this tradition or injunction by the disciples; it seems, they did not wash their hands when they ate bread, which was the more offensive to the Pharisees, because they were men who in other things were strict and conscientious. The custom was innocent enough, and had a decency in its civil use. We read of the water for purifying at the marriage where Christ was present (<reference osisRef="John.2.6">John ii. 6</reference>), though Christ turned it into wine, and so put an end to that use of it. But when it came to be practised and imposed as a religious rite and ceremony, and such a stress laid upon it, the disciples, though weak in knowledge, yet were so well taught as not to comply with it, or observe it; no not when the scribes and Pharisees had their eye upon them. They had already learned St. Paul's lesson, <hi type="italic">All things are lawful for me;</hi> no doubt, it is lawful to wash before meat; but I will not be brought under the power of any; especially not those who <hi type="italic">said to their souls, Bow down, that we may go over.</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.12">1 Cor. vi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen22492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22493" type="x-p"/> 3. What was the complaint of the scribes and Pharisees against them. They quarrel with Christ about it, supposing that he allowed them in it, as he did, no doubt, by his own example; "<hi type="italic">Why do thy disciples transgress</hi> the canons of the church? And why dost thou suffer them to do it?" It was well that the complaint was made to Christ; for the disciples themselves, though they knew their duty in this case, were perhaps not so well able to give a reason for what they did as were to be wished. <div eID="gen22493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22494" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Christ's answer to this cavil, and his justification of the disciples in that which was charged upon them as a transgression. Note, While we stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made us free, he will be sure to bear us out in it. <div eID="gen22494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22495" type="x-p"/> Two ways Christ replies upon them; <div eID="gen22495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22496" type="x-p"/> 1. By way of recrimination, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.3-Matt.15.6">v. 3-6</reference>. They were spying motes in the eyes of his disciples, but Christ shows them a beam in their own. But that which he charges upon them is not barely a recrimination, for it will be no vindication of ourselves to condemn our reprovers; but it is such a censure of their tradition (and the authority of that was what they built their charge upon) as makes not only a non-compliance lawful, but an opposition a duty. That human authority must never be submitted to, which sets up in competition with divine authority. <div eID="gen22496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22497" type="x-p"/> (1.) The charge in general is, <hi type="italic">You transgress the commandment of God by your tradition.</hi> They called it the <hi type="italic">tradition of the elders,</hi> laying stress upon the antiquity of the usage, and the authority of them that imposed it, as the church of Rome does upon fathers and councils; but Christ calls it <hi type="italic">their</hi> tradition. Note, Illegal impositions will be laid to the charge of those who support and maintain them, and keep them up, as well of those who first invented and enjoined them; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.16">Mic. iv. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">You transgress the commandment of God.</hi> Note, Those who are most zealous of their own impositions, are commonly most careless of God's commands; which is a good reason why Christ's disciples should stand upon their guard against such impositions, lest, though at first they seem only to infringe the liberty of Christians, they come at length to confront the authority of Christ. Though the Pharisees, in this command of washing before meat, did not entrench upon any command of God; yet, because in other instances they did, he justifies his disciples' disobedience to this. <div eID="gen22497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22498" type="x-p"/> (2.) The proof of this charge is in particular instance, that of their transgressing the fifth commandment. <div eID="gen22498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22499" type="x-p"/> [1.] Let us see what the command of God is (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.4">v. 4</reference>), what the precept, and what the sanction of the law is. <div eID="gen22499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22500" type="x-p"/> The precept is, <hi type="italic">Honour thy father and thy mother;</hi> this is enjoined by the common Father of mankind, and by paying respect to them whom Providence has made the instruments of our being, we give honour to him who is the Author of it, who has thereby, as to us, put some of his image upon them. The whole of children's duty to their parents is included in this of honouring them, which is the spring and foundation of all the rest, <hi type="italic">If I be a father, where is my honour?</hi> Our Saviour here supposes it to mean the duty of children's maintaining their parents, and ministering to their wants, if there be occasion, and being every way serviceable to their comfort. <hi type="italic">Honour widows,</hi> that is, maintain them, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1 Tim. v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen22500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22501" type="x-p"/> The sanction of this law in the fifth commandment, is, a promise, <hi type="italic">that thy days may be long;</hi> but our Saviour waives that, lest any should thence infer it to be only a thing commendable and profitable, and insists upon the penalty annexed to the breach of this commandment in another scripture, which denotes the duty to be highly and indispensably necessary; <hi type="italic">He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death:</hi> this law we have, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Exod. xxi. 17</reference>. The sin of cursing parents is here opposed to the duty of honouring them. Those who speak ill of their parents, or wish ill to them, who mock at them, or give them taunting and opprobrious language, break this law. If to call a brother <hi type="italic">Raca</hi> be so penal, what is it to call a father so? By our Saviour's application of this law, it appears, that denying service or relief to parents is included in cursing them. Though the language be respectful enough, and nothing abusive in it, yet what will that avail, if the deeds be not agreeable? it is but like him that said, <hi type="italic">I go, Sir, and went not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.30">ch. xxi. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen22501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22502" type="x-p"/> [2.] Let us see what was the contradiction which the tradition of the elders gave to this command. It was not direct and downright, but implicit; their casuists gave them such rules as furnished them with an easy evasion from the obligation of this command, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.5-Matt.15.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. You hear what God saith, <hi type="italic">but ye say</hi> so and so. Note, That which men say, even great men, and learned men, and men in authority, must be examined by that which God saith; and if it be found either contrary or inconsistent, it may and must be rejected, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.19">Acts iv. 19</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen22502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22503" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What their tradition was; That a man could not in any case bestow his worldly estate better than to give it to the priests, and devote it to the service of the temple: and that when any thing was so devoted, it was not only unlawful to alienate it, but all other obligations, though ever so just and sacred, were thereby superseded, and a man was thereby discharged from them. And this proceeded partly from their ceremoniousness, and the superstitious regard they had to the temple, and partly from their covetousness, and love of money: for what was given to the temple they were gainers by. The former was, in pretence, the latter was, in truth, at the bottom of this tradition. <div eID="gen22503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22504" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How they allowed the application of this to the case of children. When their parents' necessities called for their assistance, they pleaded, that all they could spare from themselves and their children, they had devoted to the treasury of the temple; <hi type="italic">It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me,</hi> and therefore their parents must expect nothing from them; suggesting withal, that the spiritual advantage of what was so devoted, would redound to the parents, who must live upon that air. This, they taught, was a good and valid plea, and many undutiful, unnatural children made use of it, and they justified them in it, and said, <hi type="italic">He shall be free;</hi> so we supply the sense. Some go further, and supply it thus, "<hi type="italic">He doth well, his days shall be long in the land,</hi> and he shall be looked upon as having duly observed the fifth commandment." The pretence of religion would make his refusal to provide for his parents not only passable but plausible. But the absurdity and impiety of this tradition were very evident: for revealed religion was intended to improve, not to overthrow, natural religion; one of the fundamental laws of which is this of honouring our parents; and had they known what that meant, <hi type="italic">I will have justice, and mercy, and not sacrifice,</hi> they had not thus made the most arbitrary rituals destructive of the most necessary morals. This was <hi type="italic">making the command of God of no effect.</hi> Note, Whatever leads to, or countenances, disobedience, does, in effect, make void the command; and they that take upon them to dispense with God's law, do, in Christ's account, repeal and disannul it. To break the law is bad, but to <hi type="italic">teach men so,</hi> as the scribes and Pharisees did, is much worse, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.19">ch. v. 19</reference>. To what purpose is the command given, if it be not obeyed? The rule is, as to us, of none effect, if we be not ruled by it. <hi type="italic">It is time for thee, Lord, to work;</hi> high time for the great Reformer, the great Refiner, to appear; for they have <hi type="italic">made void thy law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.126">Ps. cxix. 126</reference>); not only sinned <hi type="italic">against</hi> the commandment, but, as far as in them lay, sinned <hi type="italic">away</hi> the commandment. But, thanks be to God, in spite of them and all their traditions, the command stands in full force, power, and virtue. <div eID="gen22504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22505" type="x-p"/> 2. The other part of Christ's answer is by way of reprehension; and that which he here charges them with, is hypocrisy; <hi type="italic">Ye hypocrites,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.7">v. 7</reference>. Note, It is the prerogative of him who searcheth the heart, and knows what is in man, to pronounce who are hypocrites. The eye of man can perceive open profaneness, but it is only the eye of Christ that can discern hypocrisy, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.15">Luke xvi. 15</reference>. And as it is a sin which his eye discovers, so it is a sin which of all others his soul hates. <div eID="gen22505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22506" type="x-p"/> Now Christ fetches his reproof from <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Isa. xxix. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Well did Esaias prophesy of you.</hi> Isaiah spoke it of the men of that generation to which he prophesied, yet Christ applies it to these scribes and Pharisees. Note, The reproofs of sin and sinners, which we find in scripture, were designed to reach the like persons and practices to the end of the world; for they are not of private interpretation, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.20">2 Pet. i. 20</reference>. The sinners of the latter days are prophesied of, <reference osisRef="1Ti.4.1 2Ti 3.1 2 3.3">1 Tim. iv. 1; 2 Tim. iii. 1; 2 Pet. iii. 3</reference>. Threatenings directed against others, belong to us, if we be guilty of the same sins. Isaiah prophesied not of them only, but of all other hypocrites, against whom that word of his is still levelled, and stands in force. The prophecies of scripture are every day in the fulfilling. <div eID="gen22506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22507" type="x-p"/> This prophecy exactly deciphers a hypocritical nation, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.17">Isa. ix. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">x. 6</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen22507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22508" type="x-p"/> (1.) The description of hypocrites, in two things. <div eID="gen22508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22509" type="x-p"/> [1.] In their own performances of religious worship, v. 8, when they <hi type="italic">draw nigh to God with their mouth, and honour him with their lips, their heart is far from him.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen22509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How far a hypocrite goes; he draws nigh to God, and honours him; he is, in profession, a worshipper of God. The <hi type="italic">Pharisee went up to the temple, to pray;</hi> he does not stand at that distance which those are at, who <hi type="italic">live without God in the world,</hi> but has a name among the people near unto him. They honour him; that is, they take on them to honour God, they join with those that do so. Some honour God has even from the services of hypocrites, as they help to keep up the face and form of godliness in the world, whence God fetches honour to himself, though they intend it not to him. When God's enemies submit themselves but feignedly, when <hi type="italic">they lie unto him,</hi> so the word is (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.3">Ps. lxvi. 3</reference>), it redounds to his honour, and he <hi type="italic">gets himself a name.</hi> <div eID="gen22510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22511" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Where he rests and takes up; this is done but with his mouth and with his lips. It is piety but from the teeth outwards; he shows much love, and that is all, there is in his heart no true love; <hi type="italic">they make their voices to be heard</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.4">Isa. lviii. 4</reference>), mention the name of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa. xlviii. 1</reference>. Hypocrites are those that only make a lip-labour of religion and religious worship. In word and tongue, the worst hypocrites may do as well as the best saints, and speak as fair with Jacob's voice. <div eID="gen22511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> What that is wherein he comes short; it is in the main matter; <hi type="italic">Their heart is far from me,</hi> habitually alienated and estranged (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Eph. iv. 18</reference>), actually wandering and dwelling upon something else; no serious thoughts of God, no pious affections toward him, no concern about the soul and eternity, no thoughts agreeable to the service. God is <hi type="italic">near in their mouth, but far from their reins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">Jer. xii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Ezek. xxxiii. 31</reference>. The heart, with the <hi type="italic">fool's eyes, is in the ends of the earth.</hi> It is a silly dove that is without a heart, and so it is a <hi type="italic">silly duty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">Hos. vii. 11</reference>. A hypocrite says one thing, but thinks another. The great thing that God looks at and requires is the heart (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.26">Prov. xxiii. 26</reference>); if that be far from him, it is not a reasonable service and therefore not an acceptable one; it is the sacrifice of fools, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Eccl. v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen22512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22513" type="x-p"/> [2.] In their prescriptions to others. This is an instance of their hypocrisy, that <hi type="italic">they teach for doctrines the commandments of men.</hi> The Jews then, as the papists since, paid the same respect to oral tradition that they did to the word of God, receiving it <hi type="italic">pari pietatis affectu ac reverenti&#226;—with the same pious affection and reverence.</hi> Conc. Trident. <hi type="italic">Sess.</hi> 4. <hi type="italic">Decr.</hi> 1. When men's inventions are tacked to God's institutions, and imposed accordingly, this is hypocrisy, a mere human religion. The commandments of men are properly conversant about the things of men, but God will have his own work done by his own rules, and accepts not that which he did not himself appoint. That only cones <hi type="italic">to</hi> him, that comes <hi type="italic">from</hi> him. <div eID="gen22513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22514" type="x-p"/> (2.) The doom of hypocrites; it is put in a little compass; <hi type="italic">In vain do they worship me.</hi> Their worship does not attain the end for which it was appointed; it will neither please God, nor profit themselves. If it be not <hi type="italic">in spirit,</hi> it is not <hi type="italic">in truth,</hi> and so it is all nothing. That man who only <hi type="italic">seems</hi> to be religious, but is not so, his <hi type="italic">religion is vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.26">James i. 26</reference>); and if our religion be a vain oblation, a vain religion, <hi type="italic">how great is that vanity!</hi> How sad is it to live in an age of prayers and sermons, and sabbaths and sacraments, <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> to <hi type="italic">beat the air in</hi> all these; it is so, if the heart be not with God in them. Lip-labour is lost labour, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>. Hypocrites sow the wind and reap the whirlwind; they trust in vanity, and vanity will be their recompence. <div eID="gen22514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22515" type="x-p"/> Thus Christ justified his disciples in their disobedience to the traditions of the elders; and this the scribes and Pharisees got by their cavilling. We read not of any reply they made; if they were not satisfied, yet they were silenced, and could not resist the power wherewith Christ spake.
entries.18e18dea7027566c126ab5040e3ba1c6b5d8b773: <div eID="gen22515" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">What Defileth a Man.</title> <div sID="gen22516" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And he called the multitude, and said unto them, Hear, and understand: <hi type="super">11</hi> Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then came his disciples, and said unto him, Knowest thou that the Pharisees were offended, after they heard this saying? <hi type="super">13</hi> But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up. 14 Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then answered Peter and said unto him, Declare unto us this parable. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Jesus said, Are ye also yet without understanding? <hi type="super">17</hi> Do not ye yet understand, that whatsoever entereth in at the mouth goeth into the belly, and is cast out into the draught? <hi type="super">18</hi> But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man. <hi type="super">19</hi> For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies: <hi type="super">20</hi> These are <hi type="italic">the things</hi> which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man. <div eID="gen22516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22517" type="x-p"/> Christ having proved that the disciples, in eating with unwashen hands, were not to be blamed, as transgressing the traditions and injunctions of the elders, comes here to show that they were not to be blamed, as having done any thing that was in itself evil. In the former part of his discourse he overturned the authority of the law, and in this the reason of it. Observe, <div eID="gen22517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22518" type="x-p"/> I. The solemn introduction to this discourse (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.10">v. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">He called the multitude.</hi> They were withdrawn while Christ discoursed with the scribes and Pharisees; probably those proud men ordered them to withdraw, as not willing to talk with Christ in their hearing; Christ must favour them at their pleasure with a discourse in private. But Christ had a regard to the multitude; he soon despatched the scribes and Pharisees, and then turned them off, invited the mob, the multitude, to be his hearers: thus the poor are evangelized; and the foolish things of the world, and things that are despised hath Christ chosen. The humble Jesus embraced those whom the proud Pharisees looked upon with disdain, and to them he designed it for a mortification. He turns from them as wilful and unteachable, and turns to the multitude, who, though weak, were humble, and willing to be taught. To them he said, <hi type="italic">Hear and understand.</hi> Note, What we hear from the mouth of Christ, we must give all diligence to understand. Not only scholars, but even the multitude, the ordinary people, must apply their minds to understand the words of Christ. He <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> calls upon them to understand, because the lesson he was now about to teach them, was contrary to the notions which they had sucked in with their milk from their teachers; and overturned many of the customs and usages which they were wedded to, and laid stress upon. Note, There is need of a great attention of mind and clearness of understanding to free men from those corrupt principles and practices which they have been bred up in and long accustomed to; for in that case the understanding is commonly bribed and biassed by prejudice. <div eID="gen22518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22519" type="x-p"/> II. The truth itself laid down (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.11">v. 11</reference>), in two propositions, which were opposite to the vulgar errors of that time, and were therefore surprising. <div eID="gen22519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22520" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Not that which goes into the mouth defileth the man.</hi> It is not the kind or quality of our food, nor the condition of our hands, that affects the soul with any moral pollution or defilement. <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God is not meat and drink,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Rom. xiv. 17</reference>. That defiles the man, by which guilt is contracted before God, and the man is rendered offensive to him, and disfitted for communion with him; now what we eat, if we do not eat unreasonably and immoderately, does not this; for <hi type="italic">to the pure all things are pure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit. i. 15</reference>. The Pharisees carried the ceremonial pollutions, by eating such and such meats, much further than the law intended, and burdened it with additions of their own, which our Saviour witnesses against; intending hereby to pave the way to a repeal of the ceremonial law in that matter. He was now beginning to teach his followers to <hi type="italic">call nothing common or unclean;</hi> and if Peter, when he was bid to <hi type="italic">kill and eat,</hi> had remembered this word, he would not have said, <hi type="italic">Not so, Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.13-Acts.10.15">Acts x. 13-15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.28">28</reference>. <div eID="gen22520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22521" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">But that which comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man.</hi> We are polluted, not by the meat we eat with unwashen hands, but by the words we speak from an unsanctified heart; thus it is that <hi type="italic">the mouth causeth the flesh to sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Eccl. v. 6</reference>. Christ, in a former discourse, had laid a great stress upon our <hi type="italic">words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.36-Matt.12.37">ch. xii. 36, 37</reference>); and that was intended for reproof and warning to those that cavilled at him; this here is intended for reproof and warning to those that cavilled at the disciples, and censured them. It is not the disciples that defile themselves with what they eat, but the Pharisees that defile themselves with what they speak spitefully and censoriously of them. Note, Those who charge guilt upon others for transgressing the commandments of men, many times bring greater guilt upon themselves, by transgressing the law of God against rash judging. Those most defile themselves, who are most forward to censure the defilements of others. <div eID="gen22521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22522" type="x-p"/> III. The offence that was taken at this truth and the account brought to Christ of that offence (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.12">v. 12</reference>); "<hi type="italic">The disciples said unto him, Knowest thou that the Pharisees were offended,</hi> and didst thou not foresee that they would be so, <hi type="italic">at this saying,</hi> and would think the worse of thee and of thy doctrine for it, and be the more enraged at thee?" <div eID="gen22522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22523" type="x-p"/> 1. It was not strange that the Pharisees should be offended at this plain truth, for they were men made up of error and enmity, mistakes and malice. Sore eyes cannot bear clear light; and nothing is more provoking to proud imposers than the undeceiving of those whom they have first blindfolded, and then enslaved. It should seem that the Pharisees, who were strict observers of the traditions, were more offended than the scribes, who were the teachers of them; and perhaps they were as much galled with the latter part of Christ's doctrine, which taught a strictness in the government of our tongue, as with the former part, which taught an indifference about washing our hands; great contenders for the formalities of religion, being commonly as great contemners of the substantials of it. <div eID="gen22523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22524" type="x-p"/> 2. The disciples thought it strange that their Master should say that which he knew would give so much offence; he did not use to do so: surely, they think, if he had considered how provoking it would be, he would not have said it. But he knew what he said, and to whom he said it, and what would be the effect of it; and would teach us, that though in indifferent things we must be tender of giving offence, yet we must not, for fear of that, evade any truth or duty. Truth must be owned, and duty done; and if any be offended, it is his own fault; it is scandal, not given, but taken. <div eID="gen22524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22525" type="x-p"/> Perhaps the disciples themselves stumbled at the word Christ said, which they thought bold, and scarcely reconcileable with the difference that was put by the law of God between <hi type="italic">clean</hi> and <hi type="italic">unclean</hi> meats; and therefore objected this to Christ, that they might themselves be better informed. They seem likewise to have a concern upon them for the Pharisees, though they had quarrelled with them; which teaches us to forgive, and seek the good, especially the spiritual good, of our enemies, persecutors, and slanderers. They would not have the Pharisees go away displeased at any thing Christ had said; and therefore, though they do not desire him to retract it, they hope he will explain, correct, and modify it. Weak hearers are sometimes more solicitous than they should be not to have wicked hearers offended. But if we please men with the concealment of truth, and the indulgence of their errors and corruptions, we are not the servants of Christ. <div eID="gen22525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22526" type="x-p"/> IV. The doom passed upon the Pharisees and their corrupt traditions; which comes in as a reason why Christ cared not though he offended them, and therefore why the disciples should not care; because they were a generation of men that hated to be reformed, and were marked out for destruction. Two things Christ here foretels concerning them. <div eID="gen22526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22527" type="x-p"/> 1. The rooting out of them and their traditions (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">Every plant which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.</hi> Not only the corrupt opinions and superstitious practices of the Pharisees, but their sect, and way, and constitution, were plants not of God's planting. The rules of their profession were no institutions of his, but owed their origin to pride and formality. The people of the Jews were planted <hi type="italic">a noble vine;</hi> but now that they are become the degenerate plant of a strange vine, God disowned them, as not of his planting. Note, (1.) In the visible church, it is no strange thing to find plants that our heavenly Father has not planted. It is implied, that whatever is good in the church is of God's planting, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.19">Isa. xli. 19</reference>. But let the husbandman be ever so careful, his ground will cast forth weeds of itself, more or less, and there is an enemy busy sowing tares. What is corrupt, though of God's permitting, is not of his planting; he sows nothing but <hi type="italic">good seed in his field.</hi> Let us not therefore be deceived, as if all must needs be right that we find in the church, and all those persons and things our Father's plants that we find in our Father's garden. <hi type="italic">Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jer. xix. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.31-Jer.23.32">xxiii. 31, 32</reference>. (2.) Those that are of the spirit of the Pharisees, proud, formal, and imposing, what figure soever they make, and of what denomination soever they be, God will not own them as of his planting. <hi type="italic">By their fruit you shall know them.</hi> (3.) Those plants that are not of God's planting, shall not be of his protecting, but shall undoubtedly be rooted up. What is not of God shall not stand, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.38">Acts v. 38</reference>. What things are unscriptural, will wither and die of themselves, or be justly exploded by the churches; however in the great day these tares that offend will be bundled for the fire. What is become of the Pharisees and their traditions? They are long since abandoned; but the gospel of truth is great, and will remain. It cannot be rooted up. <div eID="gen22527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22528" type="x-p"/> 2. The ruin of them; and their followers, who had their persons and principles in admiration, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.14">v. 14</reference>. Where, <div eID="gen22528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22529" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ bids his disciples <hi type="italic">let them alone.</hi> "Have no converse with them or concern for them; neither court their favour, nor dread their displeasure; care not though they be offended, they will take their course, and let them take the issue of it. They are wedded to their own fancies, and will have every thing their own way; let them alone. Seek not to please a generation of men that please not God (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1 Thess. ii. 15</reference>), and will be pleased with nothing less than absolute dominion over your consciences. They are <hi type="italic">joined to idols,</hi> as Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.17">Hos. iv. 17</reference>), the idols of their own fancy; <hi type="italic">let them alone, let them be filthy still,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Rev. xxii. 11</reference>. The case of those sinners is sad indeed, whom Christ orders his ministers to let alone. <div eID="gen22529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22530" type="x-p"/> (2.) He gives them two reasons for it. <hi type="italic">Let them alone;</hi> for, <div eID="gen22530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22531" type="x-p"/> [1.] They are proud and ignorant; two bad qualities that often meet, and render a man incurable in his folly, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">Prov. xxvi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">They are blind leaders of the blind.</hi> They are grossly ignorant in the things of God, and strangers to the spiritual nature of the divine law; and yet so proud, that they think they see better and further than any, and therefore undertake to be leaders of others, to show others the way to heaven, when they themselves know not one step of the way; and, accordingly, they prescribe to all, and proscribe those who will not follow them. Though they were blind, if they had owned it, and come to Christ for eye-salve, they might have seen, but they disdained the intimation of such a thing (<reference osisRef="John.9.40">John ix. 40</reference>); <hi type="italic">Are we blind also?</hi> They were confident that <hi type="italic">they themselves were guides of the blind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.19-Rom.2.20">Rom. ii. 19, 20</reference>), were appointed to be so, and fit to be so; that every thing they said was an oracle and a law; "Therefore <hi type="italic">let them alone,</hi> their case is desperate; do not meddle with them; you may soon provoke them, but never convince them." How miserable was the case of the Jewish Church now when their leaders were blind, so self-conceitedly foolish, as to be peremptory in their conduct, while the people were so sottishly foolish as to follow them with an implicit faith and obedience, and <hi type="italic">willingly walk after the commandment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.11">Hos. v. 11</reference>. Now the prophecy was fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.10">Isa. xxix. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">14</reference>. And it is easy to imagine <hi type="italic">what will be in the end hereof,</hi> when <hi type="italic">the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means, and the people love to have it so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jer. v. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen22531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22532" type="x-p"/> [2.] They are posting to destruction, and will shortly be plunged into it; <hi type="italic">Both shall fall into the ditch.</hi> This must needs be the end of it, if both be so blind, and yet both so bold, venturing forward, and yet not aware of danger. Both will be involved in the general desolation coming upon the Jews, and both drowned in eternal destruction and perdition. The blind leaders and the blind followers will perish together. We find (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Rev. xxii. 15</reference>), that hell is the portion of those that <hi type="italic">make a lie,</hi> and of those that <hi type="italic">love</hi> it when it is made. <hi type="italic">The deceived and the deceiver</hi> are obnoxious to the judgment of God, <reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job xii. 16</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those that by their cunning craftiness draw others to sin and error, shall not, with all their craft and cunning, escape ruin themselves. If <hi type="italic">both fall together into the ditch,</hi> the blind leaders will fall undermost, and have the worst of it; see <reference osisRef="Jer.14.15-Jer.14.16">Jer. xiv. 15, 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">The prophets shall be consumed first,</hi> and then the <hi type="italic">people to whom they prophesy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.20.6">Jer. xx. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.15-Jer.27.16">xxvii. 15, 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The sin and ruin of the deceivers will be no security to those that are deceived by them. Though the leaders of this people <hi type="italic">cause them to err,</hi> yet they that are <hi type="italic">led of them are destroyed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa. ix. 16</reference>), because they shut their eyes against the light which would have rectified their mistake. Seneca, complaining of most people's being led by common opinion and practice (<hi type="italic">Unusquisque mavult credere quam judicare—Things are taken upon trust, and never examined</hi>), concludes, <hi type="italic">Indeista tanta coacervatio aliorum super alios ruentium—Hence crowds fall upon crowds, in vast confusion.</hi> De Vit&#226; Beat&#226;. The falling of both together will aggravate the fall of both; for they that have thus mutually increased each other's sin, will mutually exasperate each other's ruin. <div eID="gen22532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22533" type="x-p"/> V. Instruction given to the disciples concerning the truth Christ had laid down, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.10">v. 10</reference>. Though Christ rejects the wilfully ignorant who care not to be taught, he can have compassion on the ignorant who are willing to learn, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.2">Heb. v. 2</reference>. If the Pharisees, who made void the law, be offended, let them be offended: but this <hi type="italic">great peace have they who love the law,</hi> that <hi type="italic">nothing shall offend them,</hi> but, some way or other, the offence shall be taken off, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.165">Ps. cxix. 165</reference>. <div eID="gen22533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22534" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Their desire to be better instructed in this matter (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.15">v. 15</reference>); in this request as in many others, Peter was their speaker; the rest, it is probable, putting him on to speak, or intimating their concurrence; <hi type="italic">Declare unto us this parable.</hi> What Christ said was plain, but, because it agreed not with the notions they had imbibed, though they would not contradict it, yet they call it a parable, and cannot understand it. Note, (1.) Weak understandings are apt to turn plain truths into parables, and to seek for a knot in a bulrush. The disciples often did so, as <reference osisRef="John.16.17">John xvi. 17</reference>. Even the grasshopper is a burthen to a weak stomach, and babes in understanding cannot bear and digest strong meat. (2.) Where a weak head doubts concerning any word of Christ, an upright heart and a willing mind will seek for instruction. The Pharisees were offended, but kept it to themselves; hating to be reformed, they hated to be informed; but the disciples, though offended, sought for satisfaction, imputing the offence, not to the doctrine delivered, but to the shallowness of their own capacity. <div eID="gen22534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22535" type="x-p"/> 2. The reproof Christ gave them for their weakness and ignorance (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.16">v. 16</reference>); <hi type="italic">Are ye also yet without understanding?</hi> As many as Christ loves and teaches, he thus rebukes. Note, They are very ignorant indeed, who understand not that moral pollutions are abundantly worse and more dangerous than ceremonial ones. Two things aggravate their dulness and darkness. <div eID="gen22535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22536" type="x-p"/> (1.) That they were the disciples of Christ; "Are <hi type="italic">ye</hi> also without understanding? Ye whom I have admitted into so great a degree of familiarity with me, are ye so unskilful in the word of righteousness?" Note, The ignorance and mistakes of those that profess religion, and enjoy the privileges of church-membership, are justly a grief to the Lord Jesus. "No wonder that the Pharisees understand not this doctrine, who know nothing of the Messiah's kingdom: but ye that have heard of it, and embraced it yourselves, and preached it to others, are ye also such strangers to the spirit and genius of it?" <div eID="gen22536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22537" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they had been a great while Christ's scholars; "Are ye <hi type="italic">yet</hi> so, after ye have been so long under my teaching?" Had they been but of yesterday in Christ's school, it had been another matter, but to have been for so many months Christ's constant hearers, and yet to be without understanding, was a great reproach to them. Note, Christ expects from us some proportion of knowledge, and grace, and wisdom, according to the time and means we have had. See <reference osisRef="John.14.9">John xiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.12">Heb. v. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.7-2Tim.3.8">2 Tim. iii. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen22537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22538" type="x-p"/> 3. The explication Christ gave them of this doctrine of pollutions. Though he chid them for their dulness, he did not cast them off, but pitied them, and taught them, as <reference osisRef="Luke.24.25-Luke.24.27">Luke xxiv. 25-27</reference>. He here shows us, <div eID="gen22538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22539" type="x-p"/> (1.) What little danger we are in of pollution from that which <hi type="italic">entereth in at the mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.17">v. 17</reference>. An inordinate appetite, intemperance, and excess in eating, come out of the heart, and are defiling; but meat in itself is not so, as the Pharisees supposed. What there is of dregs and defilement in our meat, nature (or rather God of nature) has provided a way to clear us of it; <hi type="italic">it goes in at the belly, and is cast out into the draught,</hi> and nothing remains to us but pure nourishment. So <hi type="italic">fearfully</hi> and <hi type="italic">wonderfully are we made</hi> and preserved, and our souls held in life. The expulsive faculty is as necessary in the body as any other, for the discharge of that which is superfluous, or noxious; so happily is nature enabled to help itself, and shift for its own good: by this means nothing defiles; if we eat with unwashen hands, and so any thing unclean mix with our food, nature will separate it, and cast it out, and it will be no defilement to us. It may be a piece of cleanliness, but it is not point of conscience, to wash before meat; and we go upon a great mistake if we place religion in it. It is not the practice itself, but the opinion it is built upon, that Christ condemns, as if meat commended us to God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.8">1 Cor. viii. 8</reference>); whereas Christianity stands not in such observances. <div eID="gen22539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22540" type="x-p"/> (2.) What great danger we are in of pollution from that which <hi type="italic">proceeds out of the mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.18">v. 18</reference>), out of the abundance of the heart: compare <reference osisRef="Matt.12.34">ch. xii. 34</reference>. There is no defilement in the products of God's bounty; the defilement arises from the products of our corruption. Now here we have, <div eID="gen22540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22541" type="x-p"/> [1.] The corrupt fountain of that which proceeds out of the mouth; it comes from the heart; that is the spring and source of all sin, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer. viii. 7</reference>. It is the heart that is so desperately wicked (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.9">Jer. xvii. 9</reference>); for there is no sin in a word or deed, which was not first in the heart. There is the root of bitterness, which <hi type="italic">bears gall and wormwood.</hi> It is the inward part of a sinner, that is very wickedness, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Ps. v. 9</reference>. All evil speakings come forth from the heart, and are defiling; from the corrupt heart comes the corrupt communication. <div eID="gen22541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22542" type="x-p"/> [2.] Some of the corrupt streams which flow from this fountain, specified; though they do not all <hi type="italic">come out of the mouth,</hi> yet they all come out of the man, and are the fruits of that wickedness which is in the heart, and is wrought there, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Ps. lviii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen22542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22543" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First, Evil thoughts,</hi> sins against all the commandments. Therefore David puts vain thoughts in opposition to the whole law, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.113">Ps. cxix. 113</reference>. These are the first-born of the corrupt nature, the beginning of its strength, and do most resemble it. These, as the son and heir, <hi type="italic">abide in the house, and lodge within us.</hi> There is a great deal of sin that begins and ends in the heart, and goes no further. Carnal fancies and imaginations are evil thoughts, wickedness in the contrivance (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Dialogismoi poneroi</hi></hi>), wicked plots, purposes, and devices of mischief to others, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mic. ii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen22543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22544" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, Murders,</hi> sins against the sixth commandment; these come from a malice in the heart against our brother's life, or a contempt of it. Hence he <hi type="italic">that hates his brother,</hi> is said to be a <hi type="italic">murderer;</hi> he is so at God's bar, <reference osisRef="1John.3.15">1 John iii. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">War is in the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.4.21">Ps. iv. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.1">James iv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen22544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22545" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly, Adulteries and fornications,</hi> sins against the seventh commandment; these come from the wanton, unclean, carnal heart; and the lust that reigns there, is conceived there, and brings forth these sins, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">James i. 15</reference>. There is adultery in the heart first, and then in the act, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">ch. v. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen22545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22546" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly, Thefts,</hi> sins against the eighth commandment; cheats, wrongs, rapines, and all injurious contracts; the fountain of all these is in the heart, that is it that is <hi type="italic">exercised in these covetous practices</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2 Pet. ii. 14</reference>), that is set upon riches, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.10">Ps. lxii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Achan coveted, and then took,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.7.20-Josh.7.21">Joshua vii. 20, 21</reference>. <div eID="gen22546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22547" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fifthly, False witness,</hi> against the ninth commandment; this comes from a complication of falsehood and covetousness, or falsehood and covetousness, or falsehood and malice in the heart. If truth, holiness, and love, which God <hi type="italic">requires in the inward parts,</hi> reigned as they ought, there would be no false witness bearing, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Ps. lxiv. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.8">Jer. ix. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen22547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22548" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Sixthly, Blasphemies,</hi> speaking evil of God, against the third commandment; speaking evil of our neighbour, against the ninth commandment; these come from a contempt and disesteem of both in the heart; thence <hi type="italic">the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost</hi> proceeds (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.31-Matt.12.32">ch. xii. 31, 32</reference>); these are the overflowing of the gall within. <div eID="gen22548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22549" type="x-p"/> Now <hi type="italic">these are the things which defile a man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, Sin is defiling to the soul, renders it unlovely and abominable in the eyes of a pure and holy God; unfit for communion with him, and for the enjoyment of him in the new Jerusalem, into which nothing shall enter that defileth or worketh iniquity. The mind and conscience are defiled by sin, and that makes every thing else so, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit. i. 15</reference>. This defilement by sin was signified by the ceremonial pollutions which the Jewish doctors added to, but understood not. See <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13-Heb.9.14">Heb. ix. 13, 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.7">1 John i. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen22549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22550" type="x-p"/> These therefore are the things we must carefully avoid, and all approaches toward them, and not lay stress upon the washing of the hands. Christ doth not yet repeal the law of the distinction of meats (that was not done till <reference osisRef="Acts.10.9-Acts.10.16">Acts x.</reference>), but the tradition of the elders, which was tacked to that law; and therefore he concludes, <hi type="italic">To eat with unwashen hands</hi> (which was the matter now in question), <hi type="italic">this defileth not a man.</hi> If he wash, he is not the better before God; if he wash not, he is not the worse.
entries.015803764f88ee13dbc0a26478a0de76bbc5cbf6: <div eID="gen22550" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Canaanite's Daughter Healed.</title> <div sID="gen22551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Then Jesus went thence, and departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon. <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil. <hi type="super">23</hi> But he answered her not a word. And his disciples came and besought him, saying, Send her away; for she crieth after us. <hi type="super">24</hi> But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then came she and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me. <hi type="super">26</hi> But he answered and said, It is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> to dogs. <hi type="super">27</hi> And she said, Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table. 28 Then Jesus answered and said unto her, O woman, great <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt. And her daughter was made whole from that very hour. <div eID="gen22551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22552" type="x-p"/> We have here that famous story of Christ's <hi type="italic">casting the devil out of the woman of Canaan's daughter;</hi> it has something in it singular and very surprising, and which looks favourably upon the poor Gentiles, and is an earnest of the mercy which Christ had in store for them. Here is a gleam of that <hi type="italic">light</hi> which was <hi type="italic">to lighten the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Luke ii. 32</reference>. Christ <hi type="italic">came to his own, and his own received him not;</hi> but many of them quarrelled with him, and were offended in him; and observe what follows, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.21">v. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen22552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22553" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">Jesus went thence.</hi> Note, Justly is the light taken from those that either play by it, or rebel against it. When Christ and his disciples could not be quiet among them, he left them, and so left an example to his own rule (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.14">ch. x. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Shake off the dust of your feet.</hi> Though Christ endure long, he will not always <hi type="italic">endure, the contradiction of sinners against himself.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let them alone,</hi> and he did so. Note, Wilful prejudices against the gospel, and cavils at it, often provoke Christ to withdraw, and <hi type="italic">to remove the candlestick out of its place.</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">Acts xiii. 46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.51">51</reference>. <div eID="gen22553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22554" type="x-p"/> II. When he went thence, he <hi type="italic">departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon;</hi> not to those cities (they were excluded from any share in <hi type="italic">Christ's mighty works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21-Matt.11.22">ch. xi. 21, 22</reference>), but into that part of the land of Israel which lay that way: thither he went, as Elias <hi type="italic">to Sarepta, a city of Sidon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.26">Luke iv. 26</reference>); thither he went to look after this poor woman, whom he had mercy in reserve for. While he went about doing good, he was never out of his way. The dark corners of the country, which lay most remote, shall have their share of his benign influences; and as now <hi type="italic">the ends of the land,</hi> so afterward <hi type="italic">the ends of the earth, shall see his salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">Isa. xlix. 6</reference>. Here it was, that this miracle was wrought, in the story of which we may observe, <div eID="gen22554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22555" type="x-p"/> 1. The address of the woman of Canaan to Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">v. 22</reference>. She was a Gentile, <hi type="italic">a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel;</hi> probably one of the posterity of those accursed nations that were devoted by that word, <hi type="italic">Cursed be Canaan.</hi> Note, The doom of political bodies doth not always reach every individual member of them. God will have his remnant out of all nations, chosen vessels in all coasts, even the most unlikely: she came out of the same coasts. If Christ had not now made a visit to these coasts, though the mercy was worth travelling far for, it is probable that she had never come to him. Note, It is often an excitement to a dormant faith and zeal, to have opportunities of acquaintance with Christ brought to our doors, to have the word nigh us. <div eID="gen22555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22556" type="x-p"/> Her address was very importunate, she <hi type="italic">cried</hi> to Christ, as one in earnest; cried, as being at some distance from him, not daring to approach too near, being a Canaanite, lest she should give offence. In her address, <div eID="gen22556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22557" type="x-p"/> (1.) She relates her misery; <hi type="italic">My daughter is grievously vexed with a devil,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kakos daimonizetai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">She is ill-bewitched,</hi> or <hi type="italic">possessed.</hi> There were degrees of that misery, and this was the worst sort. It was common case at that time, and very calamitous. Note, The vexations of children are the trouble of parents, and nothing should be more so than their being under the power of Satan. Tender parents very sensibly feel the miseries of those that are pieces of themselves. "Though vexed with the devil, yet she is my daughter still." The greatest afflictions of our relations do not dissolve our obligations to them, and therefore ought not to alienate our affections from them. It was the distress and trouble of her family, that now brought her to Christ; she came to him, not for teaching, but for healing; yet, because she came in faith, he did not reject her. Though it is need that drives us to Christ, yet we shall not therefore be driven from him. It was the affliction of her daughter, that gave her this occasion of applying to Christ. It is good to make the afflictions of others our own, in sense and sympathy, that we may make them our own, in improvement and advantage. <div eID="gen22557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22558" type="x-p"/> (2.) She requests for mercy; <hi type="italic">Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David,</hi> she owns him to be the Messiah: that is the great thing which faith should fasten upon, and fetch comfort from. From the Lord we may expect acts of power: he can command deliverances; from the Son of David we may expect all the mercy and grace which were foretold concerning him. Though a Gentile, she owns <hi type="italic">the promise made to the fathers</hi> of the Jews, and the honour of the house of David. The Gentiles must receive Christianity, not only as an improvement of natural religion, but as the perfection of the Jewish religion, with an eye to the Old Testament. <div eID="gen22558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22559" type="x-p"/> Her petition is, <hi type="italic">Have mercy on me.</hi> She does not limit Christ to this or that particular instance of mercy, but mercy, mercy is the thing she begs: she pleads not merit, but depends upon mercy; <hi type="italic">Have mercy upon me.</hi> Mercies to the children are mercies to the parents; favours to ours are favours to us, and are so to be accounted. Note, It is the duty of parents to pray for their children, and to be earnest in prayer for them, especially for their souls; "I have a son, a daughter, grievously vexed with a proud will, an unclean devil, a malicious devil, led captive by him at his will; <hi type="italic">Lord, help them.</hi>" This is a case more deplorable than that of a bodily possession. Bring them to Christ by faith and prayer, who alone is able to heal them. Parents should look upon it as a great mercy to themselves, to have Satan's power broken in the souls of their children. <div eID="gen22559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22560" type="x-p"/> 2. The discouragement she met with in this address; in all the story of Christ's ministry we do not meet with the like. He was wont to countenance and encourage all that came to him, and either <hi type="italic">to answer before they called,</hi> or <hi type="italic">to hear while they were yet speaking;</hi> but here was one otherwise treated: and what could be the reason of it? (1.) Some think that Christ showed himself backward to gratify this poor woman, because he would not give offence to the Jews, by being as free and forward in his favour to the Gentiles as to them. He had bid his disciples <hi type="italic">not go into the way of the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5">ch. x. 5</reference>), and therefore would not himself seem so inclinable to them as to others, but rather more shy. Or rather, (2.) Christ treated her thus, to try her; he knows what is in the heart, knew the strength of her faith, and how well able she was, by his grace, to break through such discouragements; he <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> met her with them, <hi type="italic">that the trial of her faith might be found unto praise, and honour, and glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6-1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 6, 7</reference>. This was like God's tempting Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Gen. xxii. 1</reference>), like the angel's wrestling with Jacob, only to put him upon wrestling, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.24">Gen. xxxii. 24</reference>. Many of the methods of Christ's providence, and especially of his grace, in dealing with his people, which are dark and perplexing, may be explained with the key of this story, which is for that end left upon record, to teach us that there may be love in his face, and to encourage us, therefore, <hi type="italic">though he slay us, yet to trust in him.</hi> <div eID="gen22560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22561" type="x-p"/> Observe the particular discouragements given her: <div eID="gen22561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22562" type="x-p"/> [1.] When she cried after him, <hi type="italic">he answered her not a word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.23">v. 23</reference>. His ear was wont to be always open and attentive to the cries of poor supplicants, and his lips, which dropped as the honeycomb, always ready to give an answer of peace; but to this poor woman he turned a deaf ear, and she could get neither an alms nor an answer. It was a wonder that she did not fly off in a fret, and say, "Is this he that is so famed for clemency and tenderness? Have so many been heard and answered by him, as they talk, and must I be the first rejected suitor? Why so distant to me, if it be true that he hath stooped to so many?" But Christ knew what he did, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> did not answer, that she might be the more earnest in prayer. He heard her, and was pleased with her, and <hi type="italic">strengthened her with strength in her soul</hi> to prosecute her request (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Ps. cxxxviii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job xxiii. 6</reference>), though he did not immediately give her the answer she expected. By seeming to draw away the desired mercy from her, he drew her on to be so much the more importunate for it. Note, Every accepted prayer is not immediately an answered prayer. Sometimes God seems not to regard his people's prayers, like a man asleep or astonished (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Ps. xliv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer. xiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.2">Ps. xxii. 1, 2</reference>); nay, to be angry at them (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">Ps. lxxx. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.8 Lam.3.44">Lam. iii. 8, 44</reference>); but it is to prove, and so to <hi type="italic">improve,</hi> their faith, and to make his after-appearances for them the more glorious to himself, and the more welcome to them; for <hi type="italic">the vision, at the end, shall speak, and shall not lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">Heb. ii. 3</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Job.35.14">Job xxxv. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen22562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22563" type="x-p"/> [2.] When the disciples spake a good word for her, he gave a reason why he refused her, which was yet more discouraging. <div eID="gen22563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22564" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was some little relief, that the disciples interposed on her behalf; they said, <hi type="italic">Send her away, for she crieth after us.</hi> It is desirable to have an interest in the prayers of good people, and we should be desirous of it. But the disciples, though wishing she might have what she came for, yet therein consulted rather their own ease than the poor woman's satisfaction; "<hi type="italic">Send her away</hi> with a cure, <hi type="italic">for she cries,</hi> and is in good earnest; <hi type="italic">she cries after us,</hi> and is troublesome to us, and shames us." Continued importunity may be uneasy to men, even to good men; but Christ loves to be cried after. <div eID="gen22564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22565" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ's answer to the disciples quite dashed her expectations; "<hi type="italic">I am not sent, but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel;</hi> you know I am not, she is none of them, and would you have me go beyond my commission?" Importunity seldom conquers the settled reason of a wise man; and those refusals are most silencing, which are so backed. He doth not only not answer her, but he argues against her, and stops her mouth with a reason. It is true, she is a <hi type="italic">lost sheep,</hi> and hath as much need of his care as any, but she is not <hi type="italic">of the house of Israel,</hi> to whom he was first sent (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.26">Acts iii. 26</reference>), and therefore not immediately interested in it, and entitled to it. Christ was <hi type="italic">a Minister of the circumcision</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.8">Rom. xv. 8</reference>); and though he was intended for <hi type="italic">a Light to the Gentiles, yet the fulness of time</hi> for that <hi type="italic">was</hi> not now <hi type="italic">come, the veil was</hi> not yet <hi type="italic">rent,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">the partition-wall taken down.</hi> Christ's personal ministry was <hi type="italic">to be the glory of his people Israel;</hi> "If I am sent to them, what have I to do with those that are none of them." Note, It is a great trial, when we have occasion given us to question whether we be of those to whom Christ was sent. But, blessed be God, no room is left for that doubt; the distinction between Jew and Gentile is taken away; we are sure that he <hi type="italic">gave his life a ransom for many,</hi> and if for many, why not for me? <div eID="gen22565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22566" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> When she continued her importunity, he insisted upon the unfitness of the thing, and gave her not only a repulse, but a seeming reproach too (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.26">v. 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">It is not meet to take the children's bread and to cast it to dogs.</hi> This seems to cut her off from all hope, and might have driven her to despair, if she had not had a very strong faith indeed. Gospel grace and miraculous cures (the appurtenances of it), were children's bread; they belonged to them <hi type="italic">to whom pertained the adoption</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>), and lay not upon the same level with that rain from heaven, and those fruitful seasons, which God gave to the nations whom he suffered <hi type="italic">to walk in their own ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.16-Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 16, 17</reference>); no, these were peculiar favours, appropriated to the peculiar people, the garden enclosed. Christ preached to the Samaritans (<reference osisRef="John.4.41">John iv. 41</reference>), but we read not of any cures he wrought among them; <hi type="italic">that salvation was of the Jews:</hi> it is not meet therefore to alienate these. The Gentiles were looked upon by the Jews with great contempt, were called and counted <hi type="italic">dogs;</hi> and, in comparison with the house of Israel, who were so dignified and privileged, Christ here seems to allow it, and therefore thinks it not meet that the Gentiles should share in the favours bestowed on the Jews. But see how the tables are turned; after the bringing of the Gentiles into the church, the Jewish zealots for the law are called <hi type="italic">dogs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">Phil. iii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen22566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22567" type="x-p"/> Now this Christ urgeth against this woman of Canaan; "How can she expect to eat of the children's bread, who is not of the family?" Note, 1. Those whom Christ intends most signally to honour, he first humbles and lays low in a sense of their own meanness and unworthiness. We must first see ourselves to be as dogs, <hi type="italic">less than the least of all God's mercies,</hi> before we are fit to be dignified and privileged with them. 2. Christ delights to exercise great faith with great trials, and sometimes reserves the sharpest for the last, that, <hi type="italic">being tried, we may come forth like gold.</hi> This general rule is applicable to other cases for direction, though here used only for trial. Special ordinances and church-privileges are children's bread, and must not be prostituted to the grossly ignorant and profane. Common charity must be extended to all, but spiritual dignities are appropriated to the household of faith; and therefore promiscuous admission to them, without distinction, wastes the children's bread, and is the <hi type="italic">giving of that which is holy to the dogs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">ch. vii. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Procul hinc, procul inde, profani—Off, ye profane.</hi> <div eID="gen22567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22568" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is the strength of her faith and resolution, in breaking through all these discouragements. Many a one, thus tried, would either have sunk into silence, or broken out into passion. "Here is cold comfort," might she have said, "for a poor distressed creature; as good for me to have staid at home, as come hither to be taunted at and abused at this rate; not only to have a piteous case slighted, but to be called a <hi type="italic">dog!</hi>" A proud, unhumbled heart would not have borne it. The reputation of the house of Israel was not now so great in the world, but that this slight put upon the Gentiles was capable of being retorted, had the poor woman been so minded. It might have occasioned a reflection upon Christ, and might have been a blemish upon his reputation, as well as a shock to the good opinion, she had entertained of him; for we are apt to judge of persons as we ourselves find them; and think that they are what they are to us. "<hi type="italic">Is this the Son of David?</hi>" (might she have said): "Is this he that has such a reputation for kindness, tenderness, and compassion? I am sure I have no reason to give him that character, for I was never treated so roughly in my life; he might have done as much for me as for others; or, if not, he needed not to have <hi type="italic">set me with the dogs of his flock.</hi> I am not a dog, I am a woman, and an honest woman, and a woman in misery; and I am sure it is not meet to call me a <hi type="italic">dog.</hi>" No, here is not a word of this. Note, A humble, believing soul, that truly loves Christ, takes every thing in good part that he saith and doeth, and puts the best construction upon it. <div eID="gen22568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22569" type="x-p"/> She breaks through all these discouragements, <div eID="gen22569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22570" type="x-p"/> (1.) With a holy earnestness of desire in prosecuting her petition. This appeared upon the former repulse (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.25">v. 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then came she, and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me.</hi> [1.] She continued to pray. What Christ said, silenced the disciples; you hear no more of them; they took the answer, but the woman did not. Note, The more sensibly we feel the burthen, the more resolutely we should pray for the removal of it. <hi type="italic">And it is the will of God that we should continue instant in prayer, should always pray, and not faint.</hi> [2.] She improved in prayer. Instead of blaming Christ, or charging him with unkindness, she seems rather to suspect herself, and lay the fault upon herself. She fears lest, in her first address, she had not been humble and reverent enough, and therefore now <hi type="italic">she came, and worshipped him,</hi> and paid him more respect than she had done; or she fears that she had not been earnest enough, and therefore now she cries, <hi type="italic">Lord, help me.</hi> Note, When the answers of prayer are deferred, God is thereby teaching us to pray more, and pray better. It is then time to enquire wherein we have come short in our former prayers, that what has been amiss may be amended for the future. Disappointments in the success of prayer, must be excitements to the duty of prayer. Christ, in his agony, <hi type="italic">prayed more earnestly.</hi> [3.] She waives the question, whether she was of those to whom Christ was sent or no; she will not argue that with him, though perhaps she might have claimed some kindred to the house of Israel; but, "Whether an Israelite or no, I come to the Son of David for mercy, and <hi type="italic">I will not let him go, except he bless me.</hi>" Many weak Christians perplex themselves with questions and doubts about their election, whether they are of the house of Israel or no; such had better mind their errand to God, and continue instant in prayer for mercy and grace; throw themselves by faith at the feet of Christ, and say, <hi type="italic">If I perish, I will perish here;</hi> and then that matter will by degrees clear itself. If we cannot <hi type="italic">reason</hi> down our unbelief, let us <hi type="italic">pray</hi> it down. A fervent, affectionate <hi type="italic">Lord, help me,</hi> will help us over many of the discouragements which are sometimes ready to bear us down and overwhelm us. [4.] Her prayer is very short, but comprehensive and fervent, <hi type="italic">Lord, help me.</hi> Take this, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As lamenting her case; "If the Messiah be sent only to the house of Israel, the <hi type="italic">Lord help me,</hi> what will become of me and mine," Note, It is not in vain for broken hearts to bemoan themselves; God looks upon them then, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jer. xxxi. 18</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As begging grace to assist her in this hour of temptation. She found it hard to keep up her faith when it was thus frowned upon, and therefore prays, "<hi type="italic">Lord, help me;</hi> Lord, strengthen my faith now; <hi type="italic">Lord, let thy right hand uphold me,</hi> while my soul is <hi type="italic">following hard after thee,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Ps. lxiii. 8</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> As enforcing her original request, "<hi type="italic">Lord, help me;</hi> Lord, give me what I come for." She believed that Christ could and would help her, though she was not of the house of Israel; else she would have dropt her petition. Still she keeps up good thoughts of Christ, and will not quit her hold. <hi type="italic">Lord, help me,</hi> is a good prayer, if well put up; and it is pity that it should be turned into a byword, and that we should take God's name in vain in it. <div eID="gen22570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22571" type="x-p"/> (2.) With a holy skilfulness of faith, suggesting a very surprising plea. Christ had placed the Jews with the children, <hi type="italic">as olive-plants round about</hi> God's <hi type="italic">table,</hi> and had put the Gentiles with the dogs, under the table; and she doth not deny the aptness of the similitude.
