Note, There is nothing got by contradicting any word of Christ, though it bear ever so hard upon us. But this poor woman, since she cannot object against it, resolves to make the best of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.27">v. 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">Truth, Lord, yet the dogs eat of the crumbs.</hi> Now, here, <div eID="gen22571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22572" type="x-p"/> [1.] Her acknowledgment was very humble: <hi type="italic">Truth, Lord.</hi> Note, You cannot speak so meanly and slightly of a humble believer, but he is ready to speak as meanly and slightly of himself. Some that seem to dispraise and disparage themselves, will yet take it as an affront if others do so too; but one that is humbled aright, will subscribe to the most abasing challenges, and not call them abusing ones. "<hi type="italic">Truth, Lord;</hi> I cannot deny it; I am a dog, and have no right to the children's bread." David, <hi type="italic">Thou hast done foolishly, very foolishly; Truth, Lord.</hi> Asaph, Thou <hi type="italic">hast been as a beast before God; Truth, Lord.</hi> Agur, Thou art <hi type="italic">more brutish than any man; Truth, Lord.</hi> Paul, Thou hast been <hi type="italic">the chief of sinners, art less than the least of saints, not meet to be called an apostle; Truth, Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen22572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22573" type="x-p"/> [2.] Her improvement of this into a plea was very ingenious; <hi type="italic">Yet the dogs eat of the crumbs.</hi> It was by a singular acumen, and spiritual quickness and sagacity, that she discerned matter of argument in that which looked like a slight. Note, A lively, active faith will make that to be for us, which seems to be against us; will fetch <hi type="italic">meat out of the eater, and sweetness out of the strong.</hi> Unbelief is apt to mistake recruits for enemies, and to draw dismal conclusions even from comfortable premises (<reference osisRef="Judg.13.22-Judg.13.23">Judges xiii. 22, 23</reference>); but faith can find encouragement even in that which is discouraging, and get nearer to God by taking hold on that hand which is stretched out to push it away. So good a thing it is to be of <hi type="italic">quick understanding in the fear of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">Isa. xi. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen22573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22574" type="x-p"/> Her plea is, <hi type="italic">Yet the dogs eat of the crumbs.</hi> It is true, the full and regular provision is intended for the children only, but the small, casual, neglected crumbs are allowed to the dogs, and are not grudged them; that is to the dogs under the table, that attend there expecting them. We poor Gentiles cannot expect the stated ministry and miracles of the Son of David, that belongs to the Jews; but they begin now to be weary of their meat, and to play with it, they find fault with it, and crumble it away; surely then some of the broken meat may fall to a poor Gentile; "I beg a cure by the by, which is but a crumb, though of the same precious bread, yet but a small inconsiderable piece, compared with the loaves which they have." Note, When we are ready to surfeit on the children's bread, we should remember how many there are, that would be glad of the crumbs. Our broken meat in spiritual privileges, would be a feast to many a soul; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.42">Acts xiii. 42</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen22574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22575" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Her humility and necessity made her glad of crumbs. Those who are conscious to themselves that they deserve nothing, will be thankful for any thing; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> we are prepared for the greatest of God's mercies, when we see ourselves less than the least of them. The least of Christ is precious to a believer, and the very crumbs of the bread of life. <div eID="gen22575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Her faith encouraged her to expect these crumbs. Why should it not be at Christ's table as at a great man's, where the dogs are fed as sure as the children? Observe, She calls it their <hi type="italic">master's</hi> table; if she were a dog, she was <hi type="italic">his</hi> dog, and it cannot be ill with us, if we stand but in the meanest relation to Christ; "Though unworthy to be called children, yet <hi type="italic">make me as one of thy hired servants:</hi> nay, rather let me be set with the dogs than turned out of the house; for <hi type="italic">in my Father's house there is not only bread enough, but to spare,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.15.17-Luke.15.19">Luke xv. 17-19</reference>. It is good lying in God's house, though we lie at the threshold there. <div eID="gen22576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22577" type="x-p"/> 4. The happy issue and success of all this. She came off with credit and comfort from this struggle; and, though a Canaanite, approved herself a true daughter of Israel, who, <hi type="italic">like a prince, had power with God, and prevailed.</hi> Hitherto Christ hid his face from her, but now <hi type="italic">gathers her with everlasting kindness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.28">v. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then Jesus said, O woman, great is thy faith.</hi> This was like Joseph's making himself know to his brethren, <hi type="italic">I am Joseph;</hi> so here, in effect, <hi type="italic">I am Jesus.</hi> Now he begins to speak like himself, and to put on his own countenance. <hi type="italic">He will not contend for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen22577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22578" type="x-p"/> (1.) He commended her faith. <hi type="italic">O woman, great is thy faith.</hi> Observe, [1.] It is her faith that he commends. There were several other graces that shone bright in her conduct of this affair-wisdom, humility, meekness, patience, perseverance in prayer; but these were the product of her faith, and therefore Christ fastens upon that as most commendable; because of all graces faith honours Christ most, therefore of all graces Christ honours faith most. [2.] It is the greatness of her faith. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Though the faith of all the saints is alike precious, yet it is not in all alike strong; all believers are not of the same size and stature. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The greatness of faith consists much in a resolute adherence to Jesus Christ as an all-sufficient Saviour, even in the face of discouragements; to love him, and trust him, as a Friend, even then when he seems to come forth against us as an Enemy. This is <hi type="italic">great faith! Thirdly,</hi> Though weak faith, if true, shall not be rejected, yet great faith shall be commended, and shall appear greatly well-pleasing to Christ; for in them that thus believe he is most admired. Thus Christ commended the faith of the centurion, and he was a Gentile too, he had a strong faith in the power of Christ, this woman in the good-will of Christ; both were acceptable. <div eID="gen22578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22579" type="x-p"/> (2.) He cured her daughter; "<hi type="italic">Be it unto thee even as thou wilt:</hi> I can deny thee nothing, take what thou camest for." Note, Great believers may have what they will for the asking. When our will conforms to the will of Christ's precept, his will concurs with the will of our desire. Those that will deny Christ nothing, shall find that he will deny them nothing at last, though for a time he seems to hide his face from them. "Thou wouldst have thy sins pardoned, thy corruptions mortified, thy nature sanctified; <hi type="italic">be it unto thee even as thou wilt.</hi> And what canst thou desire more?" When we come, as this poor woman did, to pray against Satan and his kingdom, we concur with the intercession of Christ, and it shall be accordingly. Though Satan may <hi type="italic">sift</hi> Peter, and <hi type="italic">buffet</hi> Paul, yet, through Christ's prayer and the sufficiency of his grace, <hi type="italic">we shall be more than conquerors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.31-Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 31, 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.9">2 Cor. xii. 7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.20">Rom. xvi. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen22579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22580" type="x-p"/> The event was answerable to the word of Christ; <hi type="italic">Her daughter was made whole from that very hour;</hi> from thenceforward was never vexed with the devil any more; the mother's faith prevailed for the daughter's cure. Though the patient was at a distance, that was no hindrance to the efficacy of Christ's word. <hi type="italic">He spake, and it was done.</hi>
entries.aefb2016ba7fa0001db1f5adb7e3eaccce2bec4a: <div eID="gen22580" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Four Thousand Men Fed.</title> <div sID="gen22581" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jesus departed from thence, and came nigh unto the sea of Galilee; and went up into a mountain, and sat down there. <hi type="super">30</hi> And great multitudes came unto him, having with them <hi type="italic">those that were</hi> lame, blind, dumb, maimed, and many others, and cast them down at Jesus' feet; and he healed them: 31 Insomuch that the multitude wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see: and they glorified the God of Israel. <hi type="super">32</hi> Then Jesus called his disciples <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> and said, I have compassion on the multitude, because they continue with me now three days, and have nothing to eat: and I will not send them away fasting, lest they faint in the way. <hi type="super">33</hi> And his disciples say unto him, Whence should we have so much bread in the wilderness, as to fill so great a multitude? <hi type="super">34</hi> And Jesus saith unto them, How many loaves have ye? And they said, Seven, and a few little fishes. <hi type="super">35</hi> And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he took the seven loaves and the fishes, and gave thanks, and brake <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and gave to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude. <hi type="super">37</hi> And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the broken <hi type="italic">meat</hi> that was left seven baskets full. <hi type="super">38</hi> And they that did eat were four thousand men, beside women and children. 39 And he sent away the multitude, and took ship, and came into the coasts of Magdala. <div eID="gen22581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22582" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general account of Christ's cures, his curing by wholesale. The tokens of Christ's power and goodness are neither scarce nor scanty; for there is in him an overflowing fulness. Now observe, <div eID="gen22582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22583" type="x-p"/> 1. The place where these cures were wrought; it was <hi type="italic">near the sea of Galilee,</hi> a part of the country Christ was much conversant with. We read not of any thing he did in the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, but the casting of the devil out of the woman of Canaan's daughter, as if he took that journey on purpose, with that in prospect. Let not ministers grudge their pains to do good, though but to few. He that knows the worth of souls, would go a great way to help to save one from death and Satan's power. <div eID="gen22583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22584" type="x-p"/> But <hi type="italic">Jesus departed thence.</hi> Having let fall that crumb under table, he here returns to make a full feast for the children. We may do that occasionally for one, which we may not make a constant practice of. Christ steps into the coast of Tyre and Sidon, but he <hi type="italic">sits down by the sea of Galilee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.29">v. 29</reference>), sits down not on a stately throne, or tribunal of judgment, but on a mountain: so mean and homely were his most solemn appearances in the days of his flesh! He <hi type="italic">sat down on a mountain,</hi> that all might see him, and have free access to him; for he is an open Saviour. He sat down there, as one tired with his journey, and willing to have a little rest; or rather, as one waiting to be gracious. He sat, expecting patients, as Abraham at his tent-door, ready to entertain strangers. He settled himself to this good work. <div eID="gen22584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22585" type="x-p"/> 2. The multitudes and maladies that were healed by him (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.30">v. 30</reference>); <hi type="italic">Great multitudes came to him;</hi> that the scripture might be fulfilled, <hi type="italic">Unto him shall the gathering of the people be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>. If Christ's ministers could cure bodily diseases as Christ did, there would be more flocking to them than there is; we are soon sensible of bodily pain and sickness, but few are concerned about their souls and their spiritual diseases. <div eID="gen22585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22586" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) Such was the goodness of Christ, that he admitted all sorts of people; the poor as well as the rich are welcome to Christ, and with him there is room enough for all comers. He never complained of crowds or throngs of seekers, or looked with contempt upon the vulgar, the <hi type="italic">herd,</hi> as they are called; for the souls of peasants are as precious with him as the souls of princes. <div eID="gen22586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22587" type="x-p"/> (2.) Such was the power of Christ, that he healed all sorts of diseases; those that came to him, brought their sick relations and friends along with them, and <hi type="italic">cast them down at Jesus' feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.30">v. 30</reference>. We read not of any thing they said to him, but they laid them down before him as objects of pity, to be looked upon by him. Their calamities spake more for them than the tongue of the most eloquent orator could. <hi type="italic">David showed before God his trouble,</hi> that was enough, he then left it with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.2">Ps. cxlii. 2</reference>. Whatever our case is, the only way to find ease and relief, is, to lay it at Christ's feet, to spread it before him, and refer it to his cognizance, and then submit it to him, and refer it to his disposal. Those that would have spiritual healing from Christ, must lay themselves at his feet, to be ruled and ordered as he pleaseth. <div eID="gen22587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22588" type="x-p"/> Here were <hi type="italic">lame, blind, dumb, maimed, and many others,</hi> brought to Christ. See what work sin has made! It has turned the world into a hospital: what various diseases are human bodies subject to! See what work the Saviour makes! He conquers those hosts of enemies to mankind. Here were such diseases as a flame of fancy could contribute neither to the cause of nor to the cure of; as lying not in the humours, but in the members of the body; and yet these were subject to the commands of Christ. <hi type="italic">He sent his word, and healed them.</hi> Note, All diseases are at the command of Christ, to go and come as he bids them. This is an instance of Christ's power, which may comfort us in all our weaknesses; and of his pity, which may comfort us in all our miseries. <div eID="gen22588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22589" type="x-p"/> 3. The influence that this had upon the people, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.31">v. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen22589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22590" type="x-p"/> (1.) They <hi type="italic">wondered,</hi> and well they might. Christ's works should be our wonder. <hi type="italic">It is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.23">Ps. cxviii. 23</reference>. The spiritual cures that Christ works are wonderful. When blind souls are made to see by faith, <hi type="italic">the dumb to speak</hi> in prayer, <hi type="italic">the lame to walk</hi> in holy obedience, it is to be wondered at. <hi type="italic">Sing unto the Lord a new song, for</hi> thus <hi type="italic">he has done marvellous things.</hi> <div eID="gen22590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22591" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">They glorified the God of Israel,</hi> whom the Pharisees, when they saw these things, blasphemed. Miracles, which are the matter of our wonder, must be the matter of our praise; and mercies, which are the matter of our rejoicing, must be the matter of our thanksgiving. Those that were healed, glorified God; if he heal our diseases, all that is within us must bless his holy name; and if we have been graciously preserved from blindness, and lameness, and dumbness, we have as much reason to bless God as if we had been cured of them; nay, and the standers-by glorified God. Note, God must be acknowledged with praise and thankfulness in the mercies of others as in our own. <hi type="italic">They glorified</hi> him as <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> his church's God, a God in covenant with his people, who hath sent the Messiah promised; and this is he. See <reference osisRef="Luke.1.68">Luke i. 68</reference>. <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.</hi> This was done by the power of the God of Israel, and no other could do it. <div eID="gen22591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22592" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a particular account of his feeding <hi type="italic">four thousand men</hi> with <hi type="italic">seven loaves, and a few little fishes,</hi> as he had lately fed <hi type="italic">five thousand with five loaves.</hi> The guests indeed were now not quite so many as then, and the provision a little more; which does not intimate that Christ's arm was shortened, but that he wrought his miracles as the occasion required, and not for ostentation, and therefore he suited them to the occasion: both then and now he took as many as were to be fed, and made use of all that was at hand to feed them with. When once the utmost powers of nature are exceeded, we must say, <hi type="italic">This is the finger of God;</hi> and it is neither here nor there how far they are outdone; so that this is no less a miracle than the former. <div eID="gen22592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22593" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Christ's pity (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.32">v. 32</reference>); <hi type="italic">I have compassion on the multitude.</hi> He tells his disciples this, both to try and to excite their compassion. When he was about to work this miracle, he called them to him, and made them acquainted with his purpose, and discoursed with them about it; not because he needed their advice, but because he would give an instance of his condescending love to them. He called them not <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the servant knows not what his Lord doeth,</hi> but treated them as his friends and counsellors. <hi type="italic">Shall I hide from Abraham the thing that I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Gen. xviii. 17</reference>. In what he said to them, Observe, <div eID="gen22593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22594" type="x-p"/> (1.) The case of the multitude; <hi type="italic">They continue with me now three days, and have nothing to eat.</hi> This is an instance of their zeal, and the strength of their affection to Christ and his word, that they not only left their callings, to attend upon him on week-days, but underwent a deal of hardship, to continue with him; they wanted their natural rest, and, for aught that appeared, lay like soldiers in the field; they wanted necessary food, and had scarcely enough to keep life and soul together. In those hotter countries they could better bear long fasting than we can in these colder climates: but though it could not but be grievous to the body, and might endanger their health, yet <hi type="italic">the zeal of God's house thus ate them up,</hi> and they esteemed the words of Christ more than their necessary food. We think three hours too much to attend upon public ordinances; but these people staid together three days, and yet snuffed not at it, nor said, <hi type="italic">Behold, what a weariness is it!</hi> Observe, With what tenderness Christ spoke of it; <hi type="italic">I have compassion on them.</hi> It had become them to have compassion on him, who took so much pains with them for three days together, and was so indefatigable in teaching and healing; so much virtue had gone out of him, and yet for aught that appears he was fasting too: but he prevented them with his compassion. Note, Our Lord Jesus keeps an account how long his followers continue their attendance on him, and takes notice of the difficulty they sustain in it (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Rev. ii. 2</reference>); <hi type="italic">I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience:</hi> and it shall <hi type="italic">in no wise lose its reward.</hi> <div eID="gen22594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22595" type="x-p"/> Now the exigence the people were reduced to serves to magnify. [1.] The mercy of their supply: he fed them when they were hungry; and then food was doubly welcome. He treated them as he did Israel of old; <hi type="italic">he suffered them to hunger, and then fed them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.3">Deut. viii. 3</reference>); for that is <hi type="italic">sweet to the hungry soul,</hi> which <hi type="italic">the full soul loathes.</hi> [2.] The miracle of their supply: having been so long fasting, their appetites were the more craving. If two hungry meals make the third a glutton, what would three hungry days do? And yet <hi type="italic">they did all eat and were filled.</hi> Note, There are mercy and grace enough with Christ, to give the most earnest and enlarged desire an abundant satisfaction; <hi type="italic">Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it. He replenisheth even the hungry soul.</hi> <div eID="gen22595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22596" type="x-p"/> (2.) The care of our master concerning them; <hi type="italic">I will not send them away fasting, lest they should faint by the way;</hi> which would be a discredit to Christ and his family, and a discouragement both to them and to others. Note, It is the unhappiness of our present state, that when our souls are in some measure elevated and enlarged, our bodies cannot keep pace with them in good duties. The weakness of the flesh is a great grievance to the willingness of the spirit. It will not be so in heaven, where the body shall be made spiritual, where <hi type="italic">they rest not, day and night, from praising God,</hi> and yet faint not; where <hi type="italic">they hunger no more, nor thirst any more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.16">Rev. vii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen22596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22597" type="x-p"/> Here is, 2. Christ's power. His pity of their wants sets his power on work for their supply. Now observe, <div eID="gen22597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22598" type="x-p"/> (1.) How his power was distrusted by his disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.23">v. 23</reference>); <hi type="italic">whence should we have so much bread in the wilderness?</hi> A proper question, one would think, like that of Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.11.22">Num. xi. 22</reference>). <hi type="italic">Shall the flocks and the herds be slain to suffice them?</hi> But it was here an improper question, considering not only the general assurance the disciples had of the power of Christ, but the particular experience they lately had of a seasonable and sufficient provision by miracle in a like case; they had been not only the witnesses, but the ministers, of the former miracle; the multiplied bread went through their hands; so that it was an instance of great weakness for them to ask, <hi type="italic">Whence shall we have bread?</hi> Could they be at a loss, while they had their Master with them? Note, Forgetting former experiences leaves us under present doubts. <div eID="gen22598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22599" type="x-p"/> Christ knew how slender the provision was, but he would know it from them (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.34">v. 34</reference>); <hi type="italic">How many loaves have ye?</hi> Before he would work, he would have it seen how little he had to work on, that his power might shine the brighter. What they had, they had for themselves, and it was little enough for their own family; but Christ would have them bestow it all upon the multitude, and trust Providence for more. Note, it becomes Christ's disciples to be generous, their Master was so: what we have, we should be free of, as there is occasion; <hi type="italic">given to hospitality;</hi> not like Nabal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.11">1 Sam. xxv. 11</reference>), but like Elisha, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42">2 Kings iv. 42</reference>. Niggardliness to-day, out of thoughtfulness for to-morrow, is a complication of corrupt affection that ought to be mortified. If we be prudently kind and charitable with what we have, we may piously hope that God will send more. <hi type="italic">Jehovah-jireh, The Lord will provide.</hi> The disciples asked, <hi type="italic">Whence should we have bread?</hi> Christ asked, <hi type="italic">How many loaves have ye?</hi> Note, When we cannot have what we would, we must make the best of what we have, and do good with it as far as it will go; we must not think so much of our wants as of our havings. Christ herein went according to the rule he gave to Martha, not to be <hi type="italic">troubled about many things, nor cumbered about much serving.</hi> Nature is content with little, grace with less, but lust with nothing. <div eID="gen22599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22600" type="x-p"/> (2.) How his power was discovered to the multitude, in the plentiful provision he made for them; the manner of which is much the same as before, <reference osisRef="Matt.14.18">ch. xiv. 18</reference>, &c. Observe here, <div eID="gen22600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22601" type="x-p"/> [1.] The provision that was at hand; <hi type="italic">seven loaves, and a few fishes:</hi> the fish not proportionable to the bread, for bread is the staff of life. It is probable that the fish was such as they had themselves taken; for they were fishers, and were now near the sea. Note, It is comfortable to <hi type="italic">eat the labour of our hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">Ps. cxxviii. 2</reference>), and to enjoy that which is any way the product of our own industry, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Prov. xii. 27</reference>. And what we have got by God's blessing on our labour we should be free of; for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> we must labour, <hi type="italic">that we may have to give,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen22601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22602" type="x-p"/> [2.] The putting of the people in a posture to receive it (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.35">v. 35</reference>); <hi type="italic">He commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground.</hi> They saw but very little provision, yet they must sit down, in faith that they should have a meal's meat out of it. They who would have spiritual food from Christ, must sit down at his feet, to hear his word, and expect it to come in an unseen way. <div eID="gen22602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22603" type="x-p"/> [3.] The distributing of the provision among them. He first <hi type="italic">gave thanks</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eucharistesas</hi></hi>. The word used in the former miracle was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eulogese</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he blessed.</hi> It comes all to one; giving thanks to God is a proper way of craving a blessing from God. And when we come to ask and receive further mercy, we ought to give thanks for the mercies we have received. He then <hi type="italic">broke the loaves</hi> (for it was in the breaking that the bread multiplied) <hi type="italic">and gave to his disciples, and they to the multitude.</hi> Though the disciples had distrusted Christ's power, yet he made use of them now as before; he is not provoked, as he might be, by the weakness and infirmities of his ministers, to lay them aside; but still he gives to them, and they to his people, of the word of life. <div eID="gen22603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22604" type="x-p"/> [4.] The plenty there was among them (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.37">v. 37</reference>). <hi type="italic">They did all eat, and were filled.</hi> Note, Those whom Christ feeds, he fills. While we labour for the world, we labour for that which satisfieth not (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>); but those that duly wait on Christ shall be <hi type="italic">abundantly satisfied with the goodness of his house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Ps. lxv. 4</reference>. Christ thus fed people once and again, to intimate that though he was called Jesus of Nazareth, yet he was <hi type="italic">of Bethlehem, the house of bread;</hi> or rather, that he was himself <hi type="italic">the Bread of Life.</hi> <div eID="gen22604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22605" type="x-p"/> To show that they had all enough, there was a great deal left—<hi type="italic">seven baskets full of broken meat;</hi> not so much as there was before, because they did not gather after so many eaters, but enough to show that with Christ <hi type="italic">there is bread enough, and to spare;</hi> supplies of grace for more than seek it, and for those that seek more. <div eID="gen22605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22606" type="x-p"/> [5.] The account taken of the guests; not that they might pay their share (here was no reckoning to be discharged, they were fed gratis), but that they might be witnesses to the power and goodness of Christ, and that this might be some resemblance of that universal providence that <hi type="italic">gives food to all flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.136.25">Ps. cxxxvi. 25</reference>. Here were four thousand men fed; but what were they to that great family which is provided for by the divine care every day? God is a great Housekeeper, on whom <hi type="italic">the eyes of all the creatures wait, and he giveth them their food in due season,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.27">Ps. civ. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.15">cxlv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen22606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22607" type="x-p"/> [6.] The dismission of the multitude, and Christ's departure to another place (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.39">v. 39</reference>). He <hi type="italic">sent away</hi> the people. Though he had fed them twice, they must not expect miracles to be their daily bread. Let them now go home to their callings, and to their own tables. And he himself departed by ship to another place; for, being the <hi type="italic">Light of the world,</hi> he must be still <hi type="italic">in motion, and go about to do good.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.15"/> <div eID="gen22607" type="x-p"/>

entries.c777ff039b19751301ab3e88dd2eb76fcecf79dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13631"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20">Mt 15:1-20</reference>. Discourse on Ceremonial Pollution. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.7.1">Mr 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.23">23</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The time of this section was after that Passover which was nigh at hand when our Lord fed the five thousand (<reference osisRef="John.6.4">Joh 6:4</reference>)--</hi>the third Passover, as we take it, since His public ministry began, but which He did not keep at Jerusalem for the reason mentioned in <reference osisRef="John.7.1">Joh 7:1</reference>.<div eID="gen26114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26115" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13631"/><hi type="bold">1. Then came to Jesus scribes and Pharisees, which were of Jerusalem--</hi>or "from Jerusalem." Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.1">Mr 7:1</reference>) says they "came from" it: <hi type="bold">a deputation probably sent from the capital expressly to watch Him. As He had not come to them at the last Passover, which they had reckoned on, they now come to Him. "And," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.2">Mr 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.3">3</reference>), "when they saw some of His disciples eat bread with defiled, that is to say, with unwashen hands"--</hi>hands not ceremonially cleansed by washing--"they found fault. For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, except they wash their hands oft"--literally, "in" or "with the fist"; that is, probably washing the one hand by the use of the other--though some understand it, with our version, in the sense of "diligently," "sedulously"--"eat not, holding the tradition of the elders"; acting religiously according to the custom handed down to them. "And when they come from the market" (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.4">Mr 7:4</reference>)--"And after market": after any common business, or attending a court of justice, where the Jews, as Webster and Wilkinson remark, after their subjection to the Romans, were especially exposed to intercourse and contact with heathens--"except they wash, they eat not. And many other things there be, which they have received to hold, as the washing of cups and pots, brazen vessels and tables"--rather, "couches," such as were used at meals, which probably were merely sprinkled for ceremonial purposes. "Then the Pharisees and scribes asked Him,"<div eID="gen26115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying--</hi>as follows: <div eID="gen26116" type="x-p"/>
entries.33a48e555964ab283867ec2d776f0c08c6ab4049: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13632"/><div sID="gen26117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13632"/>2. Why do thy disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? for they wash not their hands when they eat bread. <div eID="gen26117" type="x-p"/>
entries.b992e5300b13e2bd31bffc3f16b13f566511c575: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13633"/><div sID="gen26118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13633"/><hi type="bold">3. But he answered and said unto them, Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?--</hi>The charge is retorted with startling power: "The tradition they transgress is but man's, and is itself the occasion of heavy transgression, undermining the authority of God's law." <div eID="gen26118" type="x-p"/>
entries.78116a25fa05a84b854f612d67d1090ab3707ab3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13634"/><div sID="gen26119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13634"/><hi type="bold">4. For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.5.16">De 5:16</reference>).<div eID="gen26119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Ex 21:17</reference>). <div eID="gen26120" type="x-p"/>
entries.9401be0511883c12f11d54b23f291d894e940d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13635"/><div sID="gen26121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13635"/><hi type="bold">5. But ye say, Whosoever shall say to his father or his mother, It is a gift--</hi>or simply, "A gift!" In Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.11">Mr 7:11</reference>), it is, "Corban!" that is, "An oblation!" meaning, any unbloody offering or gift dedicated to sacred uses.<div eID="gen26121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26122" type="x-p"/> by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; <div eID="gen26122" type="x-p"/>
entries.be0341acab62195ea95c39a771a1d3ed83251eb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13636"/><div sID="gen26123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13636"/><hi type="bold">6. And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free--</hi>that is, It is true, father--mother--that by giving to thee this, which I now present, thou mightest be profited by me; but I have gifted it to pious uses, and therefore, at whatever cost to thee, I am not now at liberty to alienate any portion of it. "And," it is added in Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.12">Mr 7:12</reference>), "ye suffer him no more to do aught for his father or his mother." To dedicate property to God is indeed lawful and laudable, but not at the expense of filial duty.<div eID="gen26123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect--</hi>cancelled or nullified it "by your tradition." <div eID="gen26124" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc2498cfde815d1df87bbedf442a32e1a01ef6a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13637"/><div sID="gen26125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13637"/><hi type="bold">7. Ye hypocrites, well did Esaias prophesy of you, saying--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Is 29:13</reference>). <div eID="gen26125" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3ccc20b986f18698b3b34ed6ce0dbde427083f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13638"/><div sID="gen26126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13638"/><hi type="bold">8. This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, &c.--</hi>By putting the commandments of men on a level with the divine requirements, their whole worship was rendered vain--a principle of deep moment in the service of God. "For," it is added in <reference osisRef="Mark.7.8">Mr 7:8</reference>, "laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups; and many other such like things ye do." The drivelling nature of their multitudinous observances is here pointedly exposed, in contrast with the manly observance of "the commandment of God"; and when our Lord says, "Many other such like things ye do," it is implied that He had but given a specimen of the hideous treatment which the divine law received, and the grasping disposition which, under the mask of piety, was manifested by the ecclesiastics of that day. <div eID="gen26126" type="x-p"/>
entries.18eeff77314f7977a3a36ecdc48db44b9d158f42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13639"/><div sID="gen26127" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13639"/><hi type="bold">10. And he called the multitude, and said unto them--</hi>The foregoing dialogue, though in the people's hearing, was between Jesus and the pharisaic cavillers, whose object was to disparage Him with the people. But Jesus, having put them down, turns to the multitude, who at this time were prepared to drink in everything He said, and with admirable plainness, strength, and brevity, lays down the great principle of real pollution, by which a world of bondage and uneasiness of conscience would be dissipated in a moment, and the sense of sin be reserved for deviations from the holy and eternal law of God.<div eID="gen26127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26128" type="x-p"/> Hear and understand: <div eID="gen26128" type="x-p"/>
entries.c40e7d9171e29ca9b65339f915b737c51ba9ff79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13640"/><div sID="gen26129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13640"/><hi type="bold">11. Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man--</hi>This is expressed even more emphatically in Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.15">Mr 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.16">16</reference>), and it is there added, "If any man have ears to hear, let him hear." As in <reference osisRef="Matt.13.9">Mt 13:9</reference>, this so oft-repeated saying seems designed to call attention to the fundamental and universal character of the truth it refers to. <div eID="gen26129" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae1a4fa681122f1b725d7b4ace8a94471e8bdcb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13641"/><div sID="gen26130" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13641"/><hi type="bold">12. Then came his disciples, and said unto him, Knowest thou that the Pharisees were offended, after they heard this saying?--</hi>They had given vent to their irritation, and perhaps threats, not to our Lord Himself, from whom they seem to have slunk away, but to some of the disciples, who report it to their Master. <div eID="gen26130" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac9b21248184bad6d1520de8ce48e4b2586f11d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13642"/><div sID="gen26131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13642"/><hi type="bold">13. But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up--</hi>They are offended, are they? Heed it not: their corrupt teaching is already doomed: the garden of the Lord upon earth, too long cumbered with their presence, shall yet be purged of them and their accursed system: yea, and whatsoever is not of the planting of My heavenly Father, the great Husbandman (<reference osisRef="John.15.1">Joh 15:1</reference>), shall share the same fate. <div eID="gen26131" type="x-p"/>
entries.85704ab763d69f9578177e95f1bf9cea1e43d70d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13643"/><div sID="gen26132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13643"/><hi type="bold">14. Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch--</hi>Striking expression of the ruinous effects of erroneous teaching! <div eID="gen26132" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ecdf3580d97f83eeb4748e2864db53173f69b57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13644"/><div sID="gen26133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13644"/><hi type="bold">15. Then answered Peter and said unto him, Declare unto us this parable--</hi>"when He was entered into the house from the people," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.17">Mr 7:17</reference>). <div eID="gen26133" type="x-p"/>
entries.eab48848f8941a34862e285b6463070a2ca4ca5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13645"/><div sID="gen26134" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13645"/><hi type="bold">16. And Jesus said, Are ye also yet without understanding?--</hi>Slowness of spiritual apprehension in His genuine disciples grieves the Saviour: from others He expects no better (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.11">Mt 13:11</reference>). <div eID="gen26134" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d1b79edfb1a10a387bd19beceee1be351871ad6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13646"/><div sID="gen26135" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13646"/><hi type="bold">17-18. Do not ye yet understand that whatsoever entereth in at the mouth, &c.--</hi>Familiar though these sayings have now become, what freedom from bondage to outward things do they proclaim, on the one hand; and on the other, how searching is the truth which they express--that nothing which enters from without can really defile us; and that only the evil that is in the heart, that is allowed to stir there, to rise up in thought and affection, and to flow forth in voluntary action, really defiles a man! <div eID="gen26135" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0b37d7d746fac1c165cfaa8ec94b0de9a68c70c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13647"/><div sID="gen26136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13647"/><hi type="bold">19. For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts--</hi>"evil reasonings"; referring here more immediately to those corrupt reasonings which had stealthily introduced and gradually reared up that hideous fabric of tradition which at length practically nullified the unchangeable principles of the moral law. But the statement is far broader than this; namely that the first shape which the evil that is in the heart takes, when it begins actively to stir, is that of "considerations" or "reasonings" on certain suggested actions.<div eID="gen26136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies--</hi>detractions, whether directed against God or man; here the reference seems to be to the latter. Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.22">Mr 7:22</reference>) adds, "covetousnesses"--or desires after more; "wickednesses"--here meaning, perhaps, malignities of various forms; "deceit, lasciviousness"--meaning, excess or enormity of any kind, though by later writers restricted to lewdness; "an evil eye"--meaning, all looks or glances of envy, jealousy, or ill will towards a neighbor; "pride, foolishness"--in the Old Testament sense of "folly"; that is, criminal senselessness, the folly of the heart. How appalling is this black catalogue! <div eID="gen26137" type="x-p"/>
